newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia digs in heels in row over defence aide.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia digs in heels in row over defence aide.

text.p: The Bosnian government dug in its heels on Tuesday in an embarassing dispute with Washington, which wants a key defence official sacked before supplying a shipload of arms for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
The United States has demanded the dismissal of Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic Hasan, seen as close to Iran, as a pre-condition for handing over weapons.

It says the arms, part of the U.S.-backed "Train and Equip" programme, will not be delivered until Cengic is removed and a boat carrying the bulk of the $100 million shipment sailed away from Croatia unloaded last weekend.
U.S. officials, including the head of the programme, James Pardew, have voiced confidence that the issue will be resolved soon.
But in a statement faxed to Reuters, the Bosnian Defence Ministry said new conditions for the programme to go ahead, such as Cengic's sacking, had come "as a complete surprise."

"In August, President Bill Clinton certified and confirmed publicly that all pre-conditions for the programme had been met by the Bosnian government and that the Equip and Train programme would officially begin," it said.
It added that the new conditions "could give rise to suspicions developing between friendly nations which in the final analysis would not be beneficial for either of them."

It said "new conditions at this point in the game" could negatively affect the Vienna Arms Control Regime, the Dayton peace process, potential donors support for the programme and confidence-building measures in the region.
Washington has also said that disputes on implementing a troublesome defence law unifying Bosnian Moslem and Croat forces also needed to be resolved before the arms could be delivered.
Both Moslems and Croats, who fought an 11-month war in 1993, have been reluctant to merge their forces in one army.
The defence law, adopted only after the United States exerted massive pressure, created a joint command structure but failed to merge the the forces completely.

The Moslem-led army was outgunned by Serb forces in the 43-month Bosnian war and relied on Islamic countries, notably Iran, to circumvent a U.N. arms embargo. The West fears Teheran will use this to bring Sarajevo into its fold.
A Bosnian government official, who asked not to be named, hinted last weekend at a possible quiet resolution to the dispute holding up the arms delivery.

"The (Moslem-Croat) federation assembly is due to convene at the end of October and it will appoint ministers of the new government," the official said. "If the current dispute can be resolved like this, that would be the best solution to lower tensions."
